questions.question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
questions.title: Loose and strict equality
questions.direct_answer: Strict equality (`===`) compares values without converting their types. Loose equality (`==`) first applies specified coercion rules when the operand types differ. Strict equality is the safer default; loose equality should be used only when its exact conversion rule is intentional, such as matching both null and undefined.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether equality behaviour is explained through precise conversion rules.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing loose equality as merely comparing values and ignoring type.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Knowing the nullish exception and Object.is boundaries.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: === does not coerce operands to another type.
== follows the language's abstract equality conversion rules.
`0 == false` is true, while `0 === false` is false.
Objects compare by identity with either operator.
`value == null` intentionally matches only null and undefined.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `===` is strict equality. It compares operands without first converting one type to another, so a number and a string are different even when the string contains the same digits.

- `==` is loose equality. When types differ it follows the abstract equality algorithm, which can convert booleans to numbers, parse some strings as numbers, and treat `null` and `undefined` as equal to each other. For example, `"0" == false` is true, but `"0" === false` is false.

- Both operators compare objects by identity, not by recursively comparing properties. Two separate empty objects are unequal, while two references to the same object are equal.

- I use strict equality as the normal choice because the comparison is local and predictable. A deliberate `value == null` check is one narrow exception when both nullish states mean the same thing. For numeric edge cases such as `NaN` and signed zero, `Object.is` has different and sometimes more useful semantics.

sections.title: Coercion is the only operator-level difference
sections.content: If the operands already have the same type, loose and strict equality mostly follow the same value or identity rules. The surprising cases arise when loose equality must reconcile different types.

sections.title: Loose equality is an algorithm, not a fuzzy comparison
sections.content:
The conversion steps are exact but are difficult to reconstruct during maintenance. A boolean becomes a number; a string may undergo numeric conversion; and an object may be converted to a primitive. Chained intuition is unsafe because equality is not transitive across every mixture of values.

Strict equality still has two numeric exceptions worth knowing: `NaN` is not equal to itself, and positive zero equals negative zero. `Object.is` reverses those two outcomes.

sections.title: Selected equality results
sections.content:
| Expression | `==` | `===` |
|---|---:|---:|
| `0` and `false` | true | false |
| `"5"` and `5` | true | false |
| `null` and `undefined` | true | false |
| same object reference | true | true |

sections.title: Make conversions visible
sections.content:
```javascript
const input = "0";
console.log(input == false);  // true
console.log(input === false); // false

const item = {};
console.log(item === item); // true
console.log({} === {});     // false
console.log(Number.isNaN(NaN)); // true
```

questions.question: What are truthy and falsy values in JavaScript?
questions.title: Truthy and falsy values
questions.direct_answer: A value is falsy when Boolean conversion produces false; the falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, an empty string, null, undefined, and NaN. Every other value is truthy, including empty arrays and empty objects. Truthiness is useful for control flow but unsafe when a falsy value is valid data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether boolean conversion is separated from equality.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating empty arrays or the string false as falsy.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Choosing nullish coalescing for valid falsy data.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Falsy values are false, numeric zero, 0n, empty string, null, undefined, and NaN.
Empty arrays and empty objects are truthy.
&& and || return operand values, not forced booleans.
Use ?? when only null and undefined should trigger a default.
Use Boolean(value) or !!value when an actual boolean is required.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- Truthy and falsy describe the result of converting a value to boolean in a condition. JavaScript has a short fixed list of falsy values; all other values are truthy, so `[]`, `{}`, the string `"0"`, and the string `"false"` are all truthy.

- For example, `if (count)` skips both a missing count and the valid number zero. If those states mean different things, the condition should be explicit, such as `count !== undefined`.

- Logical AND and OR short-circuit but return one of their operands. `saved || defaultValue` therefore replaces any falsy saved value, while `saved ?? defaultValue` replaces only `null` or `undefined`. That distinction protects valid values such as zero and an empty label.

- Truthiness is concise for states that genuinely have only present and absent meanings, such as checking whether an optional object exists before use. At API boundaries and validation points, explicit comparisons usually communicate the allowed values more accurately.

sections.title: Boolean contexts perform a conversion
sections.content: Conditions do not require a boolean operand. The language applies the ToBoolean operation, and logical operators use that result to choose which original operand to return.

sections.title: Short-circuit expressions can carry data
sections.content:
`a && b` returns `a` when `a` is falsy and otherwise evaluates and returns `b`. `a || b` returns `a` when it is truthy and otherwise evaluates `b`. This is useful for guards, but it can hide a type change when readers assume the result is always boolean.

The special legacy object `document.all` is falsy despite being an object, but application code should not use it. For ordinary values, remembering the fixed falsy set is enough.

sections.title: Defaulting operators
sections.content:
| Expression | Falls back for | Preserves `0` and `""`? |
|---|---|---:|
| `value || fallback` | Every falsy value | No |
| `value ?? fallback` | null or undefined | Yes |

questions.question: How does Object.is differ from === in JavaScript?
questions.title: Object.is and strict equality
questions.direct_answer: Object.is uses SameValue semantics. It differs from strict equality only for two numeric cases: Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true, while Object.is(0, -0) is false. Like strict equality, it compares objects by identity and performs no type coercion.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether numeric equality edge cases are accurate.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connecting equality algorithms to real collection methods.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: === reports NaN unequal to itself and treats both zero signs as equal.
Both operations compare objects by identity.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `Object.is` and `===` both compare without type coercion, and they give the same result for almost every everyday value. Their differences are limited to `NaN` and signed zero.

- Strict equality follows IEEE-style numeric behaviour: `NaN === NaN` is false, while `0 === -0` is true. `Object.is` treats `NaN` as the same value as itself and preserves the sign distinction between positive and negative zero.

- For example, a state update helper can use `Object.is` to decide whether a new scalar value is truly the same under SameValue semantics. `Object.is(previous, next)` recognises two `NaN` readings as unchanged but recognises a change from `0` to `-0`.

- It is not a deep equality function. `Object.is({}, {})` is false because those are separate objects. I use strict equality for ordinary comparisons, `Number.isNaN` when the question is specifically whether a value is NaN, and `Object.is` when SameValue semantics are the intended contract.

sections.title: SameValue keeps two numeric distinctions
sections.content: SameValue is a named equality algorithm in ECMAScript. It makes NaN reflexive and signed zero distinct without changing reference identity or introducing coercion.

sections.title: Several equality algorithms coexist
sections.content:
Array `includes` and Map/Set key matching use SameValueZero: it considers NaN equal to itself but treats positive and negative zero as equal. `indexOf` uses strict equality, which is why `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` returns -1 while `[NaN].includes(NaN)` returns true.

The choice is therefore tied to an API's contract. It should not be selected simply because one operator seems more strict than another.

sections.title: Numeric edge cases
sections.content:
| Pair | `===` | `Object.is` | `includes` / SameValueZero |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `NaN`, `NaN` | false | true | true |
| `0`, `-0` | true | false | true |

sections.title: Compare equality algorithms
sections.content:
```javascript
console.log(NaN === NaN);              // false
console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN));    // true
console.log(Object.is(0, -0));        // false
console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN));      // -1
console.log([NaN].includes(NaN));     // true
console.log(Object.is({}, {}));       // false
```
